newsitem.title: MEXICO: For love, wear red panties; for money, wear yellow.
newsitem.headline: For love, wear red panties; for money, wear yellow.

text.p: Mexicans are superstitious at the best of times, but on New Year's Eve they go overboard.
Many will set off for parties on Tuesday wearing red or yellow underwear, carrying brooms and suitcases and ready to devour 12 grapes on the strokes of midnight.
For those Mexicans unlucky in love, the magic touch is to wear red underwear on New Year's Eve.
It is better still to be given red panties as a present in front of your lover, so the scarlet lingerie will stir dormant passions.

"Red panties are the most sought after underwear at this time of year," said store manager Gerardo Perez. He will sell around 500 pairs on Tuesday alone and has a full section of one aisle devoted to different brands, shades and sizes.
For those out of money, Mexicans swear that yellow underwear will do the trick and turn your financial fortunes for the upcoming year.
But the most superstitious await the strokes of midnight and the first few minutes of the New Year.
Carrying on a tradition brought from Spain, Mexicans eat a grape and simultaneously make a wish on each stroke of midnight.

Then, those hoping to travel in the New Year grab suitcases and run out of the house. For long journeys, they scamper around the block; for many short trips, they cross the threshold several times rapidly.
Those blighted with bad luck the previous year take up the nearest broom and sweep their ill-fortunes out of the door.

Mexicans with even worse luck place a bucket of water behind the main door of the house before midnight. When the New Year arrives they sprinkle the water outside, simulating holy water, and brush the puddles to the street to wash their woes away.
And those still worried about money, despite sporting yellow panties or boxers, rush around the party collecting 12 coins from strangers to bring them good fortune in the 12 months ahead.
Throwing dried lentils onto the floor and then keeping them safe in a jar for the rest of the year will bring food in abundance, Mexicans swear.
Lighting candles is another New Year favourite. Blue ones to bring harmony and to control bad moods and red and pink ones to fortify love.
"We are superstitious throughout the year," said housewife Guadalupe Beltran. "But in the first few moments of the New Year there is a general craziness in search for good luck," she added.
Office worker Blanca Gonzalez is convinced the New Year tricks bring good fortune. "I ran out of the house with a suitcase last year and ended up travelling throughout Europe," the 24-year-old said.
